---
title: "What do we mean by AI for science?"
---

A calculator, a chess program, and a chatbot all do something that once required a person. We are much more likely to call some of them intelligent than others. Before discussing what AI might do for chemistry, it is worth asking what we mean by that word.

We will begin with questions that sound almost too basic to need asking. What does it mean to model something? If two quantities vary together, what have we learned about changing one of them? What does a probability describe? A small change in the wording can change the question we are answering and the evidence we need. I would like us to notice those changes before a piece of software makes them easy to overlook. By the end of this meeting, you should be able to take a claim about AI in chemistry, say what task it concerns, identify an important modelling choice, and suggest what evidence would support the claim. We will practise those moves on small examples before using them to judge our own calculations.

These notes give a fuller account than we will work through together in the first meeting. Use them to revisit the examples afterwards.

::: {.callout-note title="Our first meeting" collapse="true"}

[What you would like to learn](../outline.qmd#learning-goals){#learning-goals}, [assessment](../outline.qmd#assessment){#assessment}, and [dates and teaching format](../outline.qmd#scheduling){#scheduling} are collected in the course outline. I would also welcome [your feedback](../index.qmd#feedback){#feedback}. The [setup page](../setup.qmd) accompanies our practical work.

:::

## Which of these would you call AI?

| Example | AI, not AI, or unsure? | Why? |
|---|---|---|
| A pocket calculator computes $17\times23$. | | |
| A spreadsheet fits a straight line to concentration and absorbance measurements. | | |
| A chess program selects its next move. | | |
| DENDRAL proposes molecular structures from a molecular formula and a mass spectrum. | | |
| AlphaFold predicts a protein's three-dimensional structure. | | |
| A chatbot writes an explanation of a chemical reaction. | | |

We begin with this comparison because the same word can hide different expectations. The useful outcome is a criterion you can explain and a more specific description of what a system does.

**Discuss:** Which examples would you call AI? What criterion are you using? Compare your choices with someone who classified an example differently. What additional information, if any, would change your answer?

## Modelling means leaving things out {#modelling-as-omission}

Before fitting a model, we have to decide what information it will receive. I want to establish why leaving something out can be sensible, and how to recognise an omission that prevents us from answering our question. A literal street map gives us a small example before we return to chemistry.

Suppose we want to walk from the lecture building to the railway station. A map that shows the connected streets, paths, and station entrance can help us choose a route. It need not record the positions of the atoms in the paving stones. Now suppose it also leaves out whether a footbridge is open. If our route relies on a closed bridge, that omission matters. The task lets us explain why one missing detail is harmless and another changes the decision.

This is the relationship I want to carry over to modelling: **we select information for a stated purpose, and that selection affects what we can conclude**. The map is an illustration of that choice. It does not establish which details a chemical model may safely ignore; we have to examine the chemistry and the intended use.

A **[model](../glossary.qmd#model)** is a representation used to answer a question about a system. A molecular drawing, for example, represents atoms and bonds. If we want to discuss their connectivity, we can often leave solvent and temperature outside the picture. Now ask for the molecule's solubility in water at 25 °C and at 50 °C. The drawing stays the same, but the requested measurement conditions have changed.

Suppose our predictor receives only that drawing and returns one solubility value. Where have we told it which temperature we mean? We have not supplied that distinction. To make temperature-specific predictions, we need to include the relevant condition in the input. Alternatively, we can restrict the task to measurements at 25 °C, hold the other relevant conditions fixed, and state that scope when using the model. Adding temperature alone would not establish that all the necessary information is present.

Here the drawing is an **input representation**: the information supplied. The **predictive model** is the rule or learned relationship that uses it to calculate an answer. These are separate choices. An increasingly elaborate calculation cannot tell which of our two requested temperatures we intended from a drawing that is identical in both cases.

This is one reason I see AI as a deeply human endeavour. Someone has decided which question matters, which observations to collect, and which differences the model can ignore. Someone will also decide whether its answer is good enough to use. Those choices shape the mathematics we will do in this course.

::: {.concept}
**Every model leaves something out. Good modelling makes those omissions deliberate and justified.**

What are we keeping? What are we leaving out? Why is that acceptable for this purpose?
:::

Of course, we do not always make these decisions consciously. Sometimes someone else assembled the dataset. Sometimes a software package has already chosen a representation for us. Sometimes we simply never thought to record the solvent. The omission still shapes what the model can learn. Making it deliberate means noticing it and being able to explain why it is acceptable.

**Try:** State one solubility question precisely, including its measurement conditions. Decide which conditions you will hold fixed and which the model must receive as inputs. Explain how one omitted condition could change the usefulness of the answer. This is the same decision we will make when preparing a chemical dataset.

Suppose we describe each molecule by its molar mass and the number of hydrogen-bond donors. These numbers are **[molecular descriptors](../glossary.qmd#descriptor)**: numerical descriptions of selected aspects of a molecule. Two different structures can have the same values for both. We have made another choice about which differences to preserve.

This question will return when we choose descriptors, describe molecules as atoms connected by bonds ([molecular graphs](../glossary.qmd#molecular-graph)), and reduce a collection of prediction errors to one score. At each step, we decide which differences the model or measurement should preserve.

There is another step between preserving information and making use of it. A representation can contain atomic coordinates without a particular model learning the relationships between them. We will return to that question through [Alampara, Miret, and Jablonka's study of text representations of materials](../reading.qmd#representation-and-model).

## The problem with the word AI {#ai-names-an-ambition}

I once offered a seminar on critical aspects of AI. I had deliberately put “AI” in the title to attract participants. After a few meetings, I had to tell them that the word was now banned from the seminar.

The problem was that everybody could have an opinion about AI while talking about something different. The word can refer to a chatbot, a recommendation system, or a machine that might one day think like a human. It gives us the same label for different tools, different capabilities, and different ambitions. Agreement becomes difficult to interpret. So does disagreement.

This is why I find it more useful to approach **artificial intelligence as a goal**: building systems that can perform tasks we associate with intelligence. The goal leaves us considerable freedom. We could write down rules, search through possibilities, learn from examples, or combine all three. John McCarthy, who [coined the name in 1955](#naming-a-broad-research-programme), allowed this breadth in his account of AI, including approaches that do not imitate biological processes. [McCarthy, *What is Artificial Intelligence?*](https://www-formal.stanford.edu/jmc/whatisai/node1.html)

AI also names the research field that grew around that ambition. But the breadth that makes it an inviting research programme makes it awkward as the subject of a precise conversation. “Can AI do science?” could mean interpreting a spectrum, choosing an experiment, explaining a reaction, or writing the report. A system could be useful for one and hopeless at another. We first have to decide which of these questions we want to ask.

[]{#what-does-the-label-tell-us}

Return to one of the examples we classified at the start. What does that label tell someone about how it works? What would they still need to know to assess its result?

Whether a familiar regression is described as AI or machine learning changes little about the calculation itself. The useful description identifies the observations it learns from and the predictions it is expected to make. Likewise, calling a system AI does not specify its capabilities, assumptions, or failure modes.

::: {.concept}
**Making the ambition specific**

- **Task:** What capability are we trying to build?
- **Method:** What operations does the system perform?
- **Information and conditions:** What knowledge or data does it use, and where will it be used?
- **Evidence:** What observations would show success or reveal failure?
:::

For example, “AI understands solubility” leaves much unspecified. A more precise claim is that a particular model predicts measured aqueous solubility, under stated conditions, for molecules outside the series used to develop it, with a stated error relative to a [baseline](../glossary.qmd#baseline), a reference method used for comparison. We can examine the data, choose a relevant evaluation, and debate whether the conclusion follows. Someone has chosen the property, conditions, comparison, and acceptable error. Those choices deserve as much attention as the name of the algorithm.

## A long history {#a-selective-history-six-stops-and-a-coda}

How did this broad ambition become a research programme? A few episodes show people trying to turn it into concrete capabilities. Recognising patterns, reasoning from explicit knowledge, and using observations to guide action were research goals long before the current generation of models. Explicit knowledge and search developed alongside learning from examples. Statistics, optimisation, available data, and hardware shaped what these approaches could achieve.

As we follow the dates, ask what changed: the question, the method, the resources available, or the result that could be demonstrated. An old question can receive a substantial new answer. The age of the ambition tells us little by itself about the value of that answer.

There is also a statistical thread: predicting an unobserved outcome from regularities in observations, and asking when those regularities remain useful. That thread does not depend on first reproducing human intelligence. Hardt and Recht's history connects pattern recognition with statistics, computing, and the ambitions of AI. It helps explain why the concrete prediction problem is often easier to discuss precisely than the broader label. [*Patterns, Predictions, and Actions*, Introduction](https://mlstory.org/introduction.html)

### Before the name {#before-the-name}

There was no single earlier name for AI, because the work did not yet belong to one field with one agreed name. In 1948, Alan Turing wrote a report titled *Intelligent Machinery*. He considered how machines might exhibit intelligent behaviour, including how they might learn. The question was already being pursued before the name we now use for it. [Turing's report, held by the National Physical Laboratory](https://www.npl.co.uk/getattachment/84156b8e-1b00-45b7-9f5e-3179cfa458c5/80916595-Intelligent-Machinery.pdf?lang=en-US)

Another important term was **cybernetics**. Norbert Wiener's 1948 book, *Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine*, examined control and communication across living and engineered systems. Feedback was central: a system measures what happens and uses that information to adjust what it does. Think of a temperature controller that adjusts a heater using the measured temperature. Cybernetics addressed a wider set of questions than making machines intelligent; it was an overlapping research tradition, not simply an earlier name for the same field. [Wiener's book, with an open-access edition](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262537841/cybernetics-or-control-and-communication-in-the-animal-and-the-machine/)

### 1950: Alan Turing and the question of evaluation

Turing's *Computing Machinery and Intelligence* reframed a difficult question about thinking through an observable test of performance, the imitation game. His paper also considered learning machines. For our course, the useful move is to ask what an evaluation actually establishes. Convincing conversation, correct prediction, and scientific understanding are different possible targets. [Turing's original paper](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~frank/csc2501/Readings/R1_Turing/Turing-1950.pdf)

**Question:** If a program explains a reaction convincingly, what evidence is still missing?

### 1955–1956: giving the ambition a name {#naming-a-broad-research-programme}

**John McCarthy coined the term “artificial intelligence” in 1955.** It appears in the title of the proposal dated **31 August 1955**, written with Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon for a summer research project at Dartmouth. The often-cited date **1956** refers to the meeting, which took place the following summer. [Stanford's account of McCarthy's work](https://legacy.cs.stanford.edu/memoriam/professor-john-mccarthy); [the original Dartmouth proposal](https://www-formal.stanford.edu/jmc/history/dartmouth/dartmouth.html)

The proposal brought language, abstraction, learning, and problem solving under that name. It already included several directions, including neural networks. A shared ambition could bring together people pursuing different methods.

McCarthy later recalled that one reason for choosing the name was to distance his programme from cybernetics. He disagreed with its emphasis on analogue feedback. This is his retrospective account of his own motives. [McCarthy's recollection](https://www-formal.stanford.edu/jmc/reviews/bloomfield/bloomfield.html)

I find this useful here because it shows that even naming a field involves choices about which questions and methods belong together. We should distinguish the creation of this research programme from the much older ambition of building machines that can perform tasks we associate with intelligence.

### 1958: Frank Rosenblatt and learning a decision rule

Rosenblatt's 1958 paper made learning from examples central to a model of pattern recognition. A threshold unit combines inputs, compares the result with a threshold, and produces a class prediction. Its weights, the numerical factors that determine how much each input contributes, can change during learning. [Rosenblatt's original paper, university-hosted copy](https://web.stanford.edu/class/psych209a/ReadingsByDate/01_30/Rosenblatt58Perceptron.pdf)

<details>
<summary>A threshold unit and the limits of its chosen rule</summary>

::: {.concept}
**A learnable rule**

$$
\hat y=\mathbf{1}[w_1x_1+w_2x_2+b>0]
$$

Inputs: $x_1,x_2$. Adjustable parameters: $w_1,w_2,b$. The symbol $\mathbf{1}[\cdot]$ returns 1 when the condition inside the brackets is true and 0 otherwise. The output $\hat y$ is therefore one of two class labels.

Learning changes the parameters using examples. The chosen model family limits the rules that can be represented.
:::

With two inputs, the threshold gives us a straight boundary. Put four points at the corners of a square and give opposite corners the same label. Try to draw one line that separates the two classes. This pattern, called XOR, exposes a choice we made when we selected the model: a single straight boundary cannot express the rule we need. Changing the weights will move the line around. To solve this problem, we need a richer way of representing the boundary.

</details>

### The 1960s: DENDRAL and chemical knowledge {#s-with-a-1969-publication-dendral-and-chemical-knowledge}

DENDRAL makes chemistry part of the history of AI itself. Work by Joshua Lederberg, Bruce Buchanan, Edward Feigenbaum, Georgia Sutherland, and collaborators used chemical knowledge and search to generate and evaluate structural hypotheses. The 1969 *Heuristic DENDRAL* paper concerns explanatory hypotheses in organic chemistry. [Feigenbaum collection publication record](https://cs.stanford.edu/people/eaf/wordpress/publications/)

::: {.concept}
**Structure elucidation as constrained search**

Observed composition and spectrum

$\downarrow$

Candidate structures consistent with constraints

$\downarrow$

Predicted consequences and comparison with observations

$\downarrow$

Surviving hypotheses and a possible next measurement
:::

The chemical problem is familiar: several isomers can share a molecular formula. The formula has narrowed our choices, but we still need to distinguish the candidates. A spectral feature may let us rule some out. Each constraint saves us from considering possibilities that conflict with what we know. The quality of the search therefore depends on the chemical knowledge we put into it, as well as on the observations we supply.

**Question:** If several structures agree with the available measurements, has the system identified a unique structure?

### 1986: learning intermediate representations

A neural network connects calculations like the weighted unit above, so that one calculation supplies inputs to another. David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams described learning representations by propagating errors backwards through a network. Intermediate units could acquire representations useful for the task, with parameter updates informed by their effects on the error. This influential 1986 publication is one milestone in a longer history of differentiation and network training. [Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams, 1986](https://www.nature.com/articles/323533a0)

### 2012: learning to recognise images {#a-convincing-demonstration-at-scale}

Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton demonstrated strong image-classification performance using a deep [convolutional network](../glossary.qmd#network-operations). Such networks learn filters applied across parts of an image. Their system brought together a large labelled dataset, [GPU computation](../glossary.qmd#gpu), architecture choices, and techniques that supported training and generalisation. Its success illustrates several developments acting together. [The original ImageNet paper](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2012/hash/c399862d3b9d6b76c8436e924a68c45b-Abstract.html)

For a chemist, the result opens an appealing possibility: perhaps useful molecular representations can also be learned. It also brings us back to the data. How many examples do we have? How similar are they? What would count as recognising something new in chemistry? We will need to answer those questions when we build our own models.

### 2017–2021: transformers and protein structures {#coda-transformers-and-a-scientific-task}

Two later markers connect this history to the course. Vaswani and colleagues introduced the [Transformer](../glossary.qmd#network-operations) in 2017 for sequence modelling. Jumper and colleagues reported AlphaFold's protein-structure prediction results in 2021, following CASP14 in 2020. These are useful examples of learned representations and of scientific evaluation with a defined target. [Transformer paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762); [AlphaFold paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-021-03819-2)

Agreement between predicted and reference structures supports a particular predictive claim. Before examining how far such a claim reaches, let us put names to the different ways these systems organise knowledge.

## Rules and learned patterns {#different-methods-can-pursue-the-same-goal}

DENDRAL gives us one way to identify a molecule from a spectrum. We begin by writing down chemical constraints: the molecular formula, possible bonds, and fragmentation rules. A program could then search for structures compatible with those constraints. Much of the useful knowledge would enter through the rules we gave it.

We could also collect spectra whose structures are already known and use them to fit a model. Now some of the relationship between spectrum and structure would enter through examples. We would still have decisions to make about which spectra to collect, how to represent them, and what the model should learn. Learning moves some of the work; it does not make those decisions disappear.

We could combine the approaches, using a learned model to guide a search through chemically allowed candidates. The same scientific task has led us to several ways of organising knowledge.

Working with explicit symbols and rules is called a **symbolic** approach. Developing models from data or experience is **machine learning**. One family of learning methods uses **[neural networks](../glossary.qmd#neural-network)**: connected calculations with adjustable numerical weights. Training changes those weights so that the network's outputs better match the chosen objective. These are **connectionist** methods. **Deep learning** uses multiple layers of such calculations to learn successive representations of the inputs. The names describe how the system works more specifically than the word AI does.

::: {.concept}
**Approaches and their sources of knowledge**

| Approach | Where does useful structure come from? | Chemistry example |
|---|---|---|
| Symbolic reasoning and search | Explicit representations, constraints, and rules | Generate candidate structures and rule out inconsistent ones |
| Statistical learning | Fit a mapping or distribution using observations | Fit a property model from descriptors |
| Connectionist learning | Adjust interacting units and their connections | Learn molecular representations in a neural network |
| Combined system | Couple learned components to rules, search, or tools | Score proposed synthesis steps with a model and search for routes |
:::

Learning from data is one way of pursuing the broader ambition; explicit reasoning and search offer others.

The traditions overlap. Statistics also studies inference and experimental design, and a search procedure can use probabilities learned from data. We will encounter these combinations repeatedly. Calling a system a neural network tells us something about one part of it; we still have to understand how that part fits into the scientific work.

We can now describe more precisely how a system works. We still need to decide what its result tells us about chemistry. That question leads from methods to evidence.

## Predicting a reaction and changing it {#what-changes-when-the-task-is-science}

Suppose a laboratory has collected reaction conditions and yields over several years. We would like to use those records to build a model. The obvious task seems to be predicting yield. But what do we want to do with the prediction?

Perhaps we want to estimate how much product to expect from a reaction already planned. Perhaps we want to choose conditions that will give more product. Both sound like a request for a better yield model. Yet the second asks us to change something in the laboratory. That extra step matters.

Suppose the difficult substrates in our records were usually heated more strongly. Despite the extra heating, their yields tended to remain lower. A model could learn that higher recorded temperatures go along with lower yields. That pattern might even help it predict another batch of reactions from the same laboratory. Now we use the pattern to recommend lower temperatures. We have quietly changed the question from what tends to happen to what would happen if we intervened.

The records contain the chemists' decisions as well as the chemistry. They chose to heat those substrates for a reason. To find out what heating does, we need to separate its effect from the reasons it was chosen.

Temperature and yield are **associated** in these records: knowing one gives us information about the other. A correlation can summarise such a pattern of variation. It does not, by itself, tell us what changing the temperature would cause. We can make good use of an association for prediction while still lacking the evidence needed to recommend an intervention.

### Explaining the model and explaining the chemistry

We might try to resolve this by asking the model for an explanation. A feature-attribution method could tell us that temperature contributes strongly to its predictions. That would be useful: we would have learned something about how the fitted model uses its inputs. The same question about the experiment would still be waiting for us.

We can see the difficulty without a complicated neural network. Take the equation $\hat y=aT+b$, where $T$ is temperature and $\hat y$ is predicted yield. Increase the temperature input by $\Delta T$, and the predicted yield changes by $a\Delta T$. Every step is visible. We can explain the calculation completely. To claim that turning up the heater changes the measured yield by that amount, we also need to know how temperature was chosen and which other conditions changed with it.

This is the distinction between explaining the model and explaining the chemistry. **Model interpretability or explainability** concerns the model's behaviour. For a simple equation, we can inspect the calculation directly. For a more complicated model, we may use an approximation or an attribution method. We then also have to understand what that method measures. Different reference comparisons and treatments of related inputs can produce different attributions. The SHAP developers work through this problem in [*Be careful when interpreting predictive models in search of causal insights*](https://shap.readthedocs.io/en/latest/example_notebooks/overviews/Be%20careful%20when%20interpreting%20predictive%20models%20in%20search%20of%20causal%20insights.html).

### Why were these conditions chosen? {#a-reaction-example-why-were-these-conditions-chosen}

Return to the difficult substrates. Substrate identity influenced both the chosen temperature and the yield. The recorded temperature therefore carries information about a decision made before the reaction. We need to account for that decision if we want to use the records to estimate the effect of heating.

One approach would be to repeat reactions of the same substrate at different temperatures, assign the temperatures at random, and control the other conditions through a common protocol. We could then compare the resulting yields. This is a question of **causal inference**: what changes when we intervene? Existing observational records can also support causal inference when we can justify assumptions that let us identify the effect. Those assumptions are part of the argument we owe the reader. [Hardt and Recht, *Causality*](https://mlstory.org/causal.html)

Suppose this experiment shows that heating increases yield. We would then have another question: how? Perhaps it accelerates the desired reaction. Perhaps it changes the balance between competing pathways. The same change in final yield can be compatible with several accounts of what happened along the way. To distinguish them, we might need kinetic measurements, spectroscopy, or isotope experiments. A **mechanistic explanation** makes a claim about that chemical process.

We began with a table of conditions and yields. We have now asked it to support a prediction, an explanation of a calculation, an intervention, and a mechanism. Each is a reasonable ambition. Each asks something different of the evidence.

::: {.concept}
**What question are we answering?**

| Aim | Reaction example | Evidence to seek |
|---|---|---|
| Description / association | How do recorded yields differ between temperatures? | Measurements, summaries, and a clear account of which reactions were recorded |
| Predictive modelling | What yield should we expect for another reaction in the intended setting? | Relevant held-out or prospective measurements, a baseline, and an error estimate |
| Model interpretability / explainability | How does temperature contribute to this fitted model's output? | Inspection of the model or an explanation method, with checks of what it measures and how faithfully it describes model behaviour |
| Causal inference | What would happen to yield if we deliberately changed temperature under a specified protocol? | A suitable intervention study, or observational identification supported by explicit causal assumptions |
| Mechanistic explanation | Through which chemical steps does the change affect yield? | Evidence that distinguishes competing mechanisms, such as kinetic, spectroscopic, or isotope experiments |
| Decision-making | Which conditions should we try next? | Expected benefit, uncertainty, cost, constraints, and experimental feedback |
:::

These questions can lead into one another. An explanation of the model might suggest a hypothesis to test. A mechanistic account might help us make better predictions. Keeping the questions distinct helps us see which step we have actually taken.

**Paired discussion:** Classify each statement below and name the evidence it would need. Which could be supported by inspecting a fitted model alone?

1. “The model predicts yields accurately for a held-out reaction series.”
2. “Temperature contributes strongly to this model's predictions under the chosen attribution method.”
3. “Raising the temperature under this protocol increases the average yield for these substrates.”
4. “The yield increases because the intervention favours a particular reaction pathway.”

<details>
<summary>Suggested discussion</summary>

The statements concern prediction, model explanation, a causal effect, and a mechanism, respectively. The second can be investigated through the fitted model and the specified attribution calculation; it does not establish the third. The first requires relevant evaluation observations. The third needs an intervention design or justified observational identification. The fourth requires evidence that discriminates between chemical mechanisms. A random train/test split and a plausible verbal account cannot establish all four claims.

</details>

### What follows from the result? {#llm-activity-turning-a-claim-into-a-check}

Suppose we have finished our analysis and are writing the conclusion:

> Our model predicts yields accurately, and its explanation ranks temperature as important. We have therefore shown that heating causes the yield to increase through a particular reaction pathway.

The word “therefore” is doing quite a lot of work. Follow the argument with a partner: where do we move from predicting yield to explaining the model, from explaining the model to changing the reaction, and from changing the reaction to knowing its mechanism?

Ask an LLM to suggest another explanation for the observations and an experiment that could distinguish the two. Then inspect its proposal. Which part of our conclusion would the experiment test? Could we obtain the suggested result even if the proposed mechanism were wrong? The assistant can help us generate possibilities; we still have to decide what an observation would tell us.

**Write for the discussion:** one revised scientific claim and one observation that would make you less confident in it. The same task can be done entirely on paper.

## What does a probability describe? {#what-does-a-probability-describe}

A reported probability can influence whether we spend time and material on an experiment. We therefore need to distinguish a proportion we have observed from an uncertainty statement about something we do not yet know. For this first discussion, the aim is to explain what a number refers to and which assumptions it needs. We will leave the calculations of uncertainty for later examples.

Even after deciding which question to ask, we may have only a few observations with which to answer it. Suppose we repeat a synthesis ten times and call it successful when the isolated yield exceeds 60% after two hours. Seven attempts succeed. We use the same substrate and nominal protocol each time. Someone asks: “How likely is the next attempt to succeed?”

The tempting answer is 70%. We can certainly say that seven of the ten recorded attempts succeeded. That is an observed proportion. Using it to predict the next attempt adds assumptions: that the attempts are comparable, that our records include failures, and that the conditions relevant to success will remain sufficiently similar. Even then, another group of ten attempts need not give the same proportion.

There are also different ways to describe what we do not know. We could treat the success probability under this protocol as fixed but unknown. We then ask how an estimation procedure would behave if we repeatedly collected ten new observations. How much would the estimates vary? If the procedure supplied an interval, how often would such intervals contain the unknown probability? This is a **frequentist** way to assess uncertainty. The probability concerns the behaviour of the procedure across possible datasets. [Stanford, *Confidence intervals*, section 18.1](https://web.stanford.edu/class/stats200/Lecture18.pdf)

We could instead assign probabilities to possible values of the unknown success probability. We state what we consider plausible before these ten observations, then update that distribution using the observations and a model of how they arise. This is **Bayesian inference**; the initial distribution is called a **prior**. The probabilities now express uncertainty about that unknown success probability, conditional on the information and assumptions used. The physical success probability need not change for our uncertainty about it to change. [Stanford, *Bayesian analysis*, section 20.1](https://web.stanford.edu/class/stats200/Lecture20.pdf)

Both approaches can be used to predict another attempt. Both require modelling choices. They need not give different numerical answers in every example, but an uncertainty statement needs an interpretation even when the numbers agree. A label such as “Bayesian” does not tell us whether the assumed experimental conditions are reasonable.

**Discuss:** What is observed, what is unknown, and what could change if we collected ten more results? Would your answer change if all three failures came from the same reagent batch?

Now suppose an assistant writes, “I am 70% confident this synthesis will work.” What does the number refer to? Is it based on repeated experiments, a stated model of uncertainty, or simply part of the generated answer? Before using it to choose an experiment, we need to know how it was obtained and what would let us check it. A percentage does not supply its own interpretation.

## Different questions about the same model {#choosing-a-lens}

The reaction example, the ten synthesis attempts, and the comparison of rules with learned patterns have addressed different questions. We bring them together because a description such as “a neural network for chemistry” answers only some of the questions we need to ask before using its results.

In my notes I use **[lens](../glossary.qmd#lens)** as a shorthand for a way of approaching a problem: the question we ask, the assumptions we make, and what we regard as an answer. The street-map example concerned which information we retain. Here we ask about the claim, the uncertainty, and the organisation of the calculation. It helps to keep three distinctions in view. They concern different aspects of a model and can be considered together.

| Question | Distinction we have encountered | What should we check? |
|---|---|---|
| Are we predicting another outcome from recorded patterns, or estimating the effect of changing the experiment? | Correlative modelling and causal inference | In the reaction records, why were particular substrates heated? Accurate prediction alone did not separate that decision from the effect of heating. |
| What does a probability statement refer to? | Frequentist and Bayesian approaches to uncertainty | Are we assessing a procedure across possible datasets, or describing uncertainty about an unknown quantity given our information and assumptions? Seven successes are observations; either account of uncertainty needs further choices. |
| How is the calculation organised? | Symbolic and connectionist approaches | Are explicit symbols and rules doing the work, or a network with learned connections? A system may combine both. Learning from examples also includes methods outside neural networks. |

For example, suppose a neural network predicts yields from the laboratory records, and we use a Bayesian model to describe uncertainty. “Neural network” tells us how one part of the calculation is organised. “Bayesian” tells us something about the treatment of uncertainty. We still have to ask whether the records and assumptions support estimating the effect of heating. Changing one of these descriptions does not settle the others.

This is why the distinctions matter in practice. If our problem is that temperature was chosen in response to substrate difficulty, fitting the recorded yields more accurately may leave the intervention question unresolved. If an uncertainty estimate rests on treating synthesis attempts as comparable, discovering that all failures came from one reagent batch gives us a reason to revisit that assumption. We need to identify the difficulty before deciding how to improve the model.

**Check your understanding:** Someone says, “Our model is a neural network, so it tells us what would happen if we heated the reaction.” Which part describes the method, and which part makes a claim about the experiment? What additional evidence would you ask for? The point is to recognise the step in the argument, then use the terms to describe it.

There are further choices within an approach. If our experiment requires a dissolved concentration of 1 mmol/L, measurements of 2 and 20 mmol/L can both become “soluble enough.” If the requirement later changes to 5 mmol/L, those labels no longer preserve the distinction we need. The [solubility example](../examples.qmd#choices-within-a-lens) follows what happens when we keep values, labels, or an ordering. It makes the idea of omission concrete in the data we prepare for learning.

For now, you should be able to explain one of these distinctions through its example and say what mistake it helps avoid. We will use them again when choosing model inputs, interpreting an error estimate, examining an explanation, and deciding on another experiment. An LLM can help write the code for those tasks. We still have to recognise which question the calculation answers and whether that is the question we meant to ask.

### What do we expect a model to tell us? {#breiman-two-cultures}

Consider a calibration curve. We could assume that mean absorbance depends linearly on concentration and specify how measurements vary around that line. We would fit the unknown quantities and examine whether those assumptions are adequate. We could also choose a flexible function for its ability to predict new absorbance measurements, without claiming that its internal calculation describes what happens in the instrument. Both approaches can be useful. What are we asking the model to tell us?

Leo Breiman's [*Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures*](https://www2.math.uu.se/~thulin/mm/breiman.pdf) (2001) develops this contrast. His **data modelling** culture starts with a probabilistic account of how observations arise; his **algorithmic modelling** culture builds a predictor while leaving that process unspecified. Both can pursue prediction and useful information. Breiman argues for a wider range of modelling tools and greater attention to predictive performance.

Breiman adds a historical comparison of modelling practices. It is useful for asking what researchers expect a model to provide; it does not replace the three distinctions above. A statistical model of observations is not automatically a causal or mechanistic account. A predictive algorithm still embodies assumptions through its inputs, construction, and evaluation. Either can be examined using a Bayesian or frequentist approach to uncertainty. The name of the culture does not settle the scientific question.

For our calibration, a familiar formula needs checking against the experiment. A flexible predictor needs checking on observations relevant to its intended use. Suppose the two predict new measurements equally well: what further evidence would we need if we also wanted to explain why absorbance changes with concentration? The distinction becomes consequential when we decide what to conclude from a good fit. The [suggested reading](../reading.qmd#breiman-two-cultures) gives useful places to begin in Breiman's argument.

## Prediction and prophecy {#prediction-and-prophecy}

So far, we have asked what a model can tell us. What happens when people act on its answer? The wish to know what will happen is much older than machine learning. Carissa Véliz's [*Prophecy*](../reading.qmd#prophecy) places today's predictive technologies within that longer history. It makes us ask why we want a prediction, whose prediction we trust, and what we do once we have it.

Suppose a model predicts which materials will be stable. We use its ranking to decide which candidates to make. The prediction has now helped decide where people spend their time and which measurements will exist. The materials we never make remain unknown. If the new measurements enter the next dataset, our earlier decisions also shape the evidence available to the next model.

A numerical answer can seem authoritative. To judge what it establishes, we need to know how it was obtained, which conditions it concerns, and what observations could show that it is wrong. Calling the answer AI does not supply that evidence. Neither does writing it as an equation.

This brings us back to the human choices. Someone decided that stability was the quantity worth predicting, assembled the observations, chose a model, and turned its output into a decision. We will make those steps visible as we build and use models ourselves. Prediction, the authority we give it, and the consequences of acting on it each deserve attention.

### The people and resources behind the model {#what-makes-these-systems-possible}

Those decisions also depend on who can build and use a model. Whose ambition does it serve, and who provides the means to pursue it? Kate Crawford's *Atlas of AI* examines the material and political conditions of AI, including resource extraction, labour, data, and institutional power. I particularly recommend it for exploring these questions further. [Crawford (2021), *Atlas of AI*](https://yalebooks.yale.edu/book/9780300264630/atlas-of-ai/)

Consider the chatbot or molecular predictor from the opening examples. Its output depends on more than a fitted function. To investigate the system, we can ask:

- What equipment and energy support its training and use?
- Who produced the measurements, prepared the data, and checks the output?
- Who defined the target and decided which observations belong in the dataset?
- Who controls access, and who benefits or bears costs when the system is used?

Take the measurements in a chemical dataset. Someone prepared the samples, ran the instrument, decided which results to keep, and recorded the conditions. By the time we download a table, much of that work may have disappeared from view. What can we find out about it? Crawford's [chapters on labour and data](../reading.qmd#atlas-of-ai) give us reasons to ask.

### What does a benchmark score stand for? {#science-and-model-claims}

A score can acquire a much larger meaning as it travels beyond the study that produced it. Our own work gives us an example. In [ChemBench, Mirza et al. (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-025-01815-x), we assembled 2,788 question–answer pairs across chemistry and evaluated models' answers. A human comparison used a subset of the questions. The questions, the procedure, and the way answers are scored determine what the comparison establishes. They do not reproduce everything a chemist does.

Now look at [TakeoverBench's presentation of ChemBench](https://takeoverbench.com/benchmarks/chem_bench). On 27 October 2026, the page placed it under the heading **“Chemical weapons development”** and displayed **66% for Claude 3.7 Sonnet**. It also described ChemBench as evaluating chemistry knowledge and reasoning. Its stated reasons for selecting the benchmark were its chemistry relevance and regularly updated leaderboard.

The heading invites us to read the score as evidence about a particular dangerous capability. That is an additional interpretation. Chemical knowledge may be relevant to that capability, but what establishes the relationship between performance on these questions and performance on the activities named by the heading? An available chemistry score is a possible **[proxy](../glossary.qmd#proxy)**: something we measure in place of the quantity we actually want to know about. Its suitability for that purpose needs an argument.

We can separate the steps:

| Step | What needs to be established? |
|---|---|
| Answers become a benchmark score. | Which questions, model configuration, tools, and scoring procedure produced it? |
| The score stands for a broader capability. | What evidence connects performance on these questions to that capability? Which relevant abilities are missing from the test? |
| The capability supports a claim about consequences. | Under which conditions would it lead to the proposed outcome? |

Changing the heading has added no new observations. The displayed percentage is a reported benchmark score; it does not by itself give a probability of a harmful event or a calibrated scale of the broader capability. Even a correctly computed, reproducible score leaves these questions open. We should ask them of our own claims about ChemBench too.

TakeoverBench's [About page](https://takeoverbench.com/about) identifies it as an initiative of the Existential Risk Observatory and PauseAI. This places the example in risk communication and advocacy. Its purpose helps us understand why this capability is foregrounded; it does not settle whether the inference is justified.

Commercial presentations give us another setting in which a score enters a broader argument. GPQA tests answers to expert-written questions in biology, physics, and chemistry. Anthropic's August 2025 announcement of Claude Opus 4.1 reports GPQA Diamond results alongside paid access and an invitation to upgrade. Its reporting notes specify extended thinking for that evaluation. [GPQA paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2311.12022v1); [Claude Opus 4.1 announcement](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-opus-4-1)

We can examine the same step here: what does answering those questions establish about the work for which we might buy access? Choosing an experiment in our laboratory adds constraints, measurements, and decisions that the question set does not test. The commercial setting and the advocacy setting have different purposes, but both give us a reason to keep the measured task and the larger claim in view.

**Discuss:** First describe ChemBench using only what was evaluated. Then examine the TakeoverBench heading. What additional claim does that framing invite? Distinguish what the page explicitly says from what you inferred. What evidence would justify using the score for the broader claim?

The [suggested reading](../reading.qmd#science-and-commercial-claims) collects the paper and these presentations. We will return to the uncertainty in finite benchmark results when discussing [test error](02-learning-from-data.qmd#empirical-error-and-population-risk). Here the first question is whether we measured something that supports the claim at all.

## From a question to a fitted model {#the-statistical-question-hiding-in-the-history}

We have spent this lecture deciding what we want a model to tell us and what would justify believing it. We can now take one of those questions into a calculation. In the [next lecture](02-learning-from-data.qmd), we will use concentration measurements and absorbances to fit a calibration curve. We will choose what counts as an error, adjust a line, and ask whether it predicts another measurement well.

Here, too, “another measurement” needs a meaning. A new solution on the same instrument, a higher concentration, and a measurement in another laboratory are different uses. We need observations that let us examine the intended one. Even observations reserved for a final test give us only a finite sample: **test error remains an empirical estimate**, with uncertainty and a scope set by the data. The calibration example will let us work through that distinction explicitly.

## Questions to consider {#exit-questions}

1. Rewrite “AI can do chemistry” as a specific task, method, and evaluable claim.
2. For a solubility predictor that receives only a molecular drawing, explain what changes if we want answers at two temperatures. What would you add to the inputs or restrict in the task?
3. Knowing that a model is a neural network, what can you say about how it works? What would you still need to know before interpreting its predictions as effects of an intervention?
4. A model predicts well and highlights temperature as important. What have we learned about the model, and what remains unknown about the effect and mechanism of heating the reaction?
5. Seven of ten syntheses succeeded. What does 70% describe directly, and what assumptions would you need to predict the next attempt?

## Suggested reading {#reading-and-references}

For an introduction to the machine-learning methods we will encounter, I recommend our review [*Big-Data Science in Porous Materials*](../reading.qmd#introductory-reviews) (Jablonka, Ongari, Moosavi, and Smit, 2020) and Mehta et al.'s [*A high-bias, low-variance introduction to Machine Learning for physicists*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.08823) (2019). The first develops the ideas through materials chemistry; the second makes connections to statistical physics. Both give us material to return to as we begin building models.

Hardt and Recht's [**Prediction and action**](https://mlstory.org/introduction.html#prediction-and-action), in *Patterns, Predictions, and Actions* (2022), develops a question that runs through this lecture: what changes when we act on a prediction? For the distinction between observation, model explanation, and intervention, I have collected [further references](../reading.qmd#claims-and-evidence), including their chapter on causality.

Breiman's [*Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures*](../reading.qmd#breiman-two-cultures) places our discussion of what a model should tell us in a debate that predates today's LLMs. Its opening distinction is useful to think with, and to question.

Kate Crawford's [*Atlas of AI*](../reading.qmd#atlas-of-ai) examines the labour, resources, and institutions behind the systems we use. Carissa Véliz's [*Prophecy*](../reading.qmd#prophecy) considers the history and authority of prediction. Both matter to the perspective taken here: AI is made and used by people, and its consequences depend on their decisions.

Wang et al. (2023), [*Scientific discovery in the age of artificial intelligence*](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06221-2), reviews scientific applications. Messeri and Crockett (2024), [*Artificial intelligence and illusions of understanding in scientific research*](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07146-0), considers how adopting these tools might affect scientific understanding. Moosavi, Jablonka, and Smit (2020), [*The Role of Machine Learning in the Understanding and Design of Materials*](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.0c09105), brings these questions into materials chemistry.

The [suggested reading](../reading.qmd#lecture-1) gives full references and access information. The [historical sources](../reading.qmd#historical-sources) are also collected there, if you would like to examine the original arguments.
